title: Two-Factor Authentication Explained: Which Method to Use
html:
Two-factor authentication (2FA) asks for something in addition to your password when you sign in, so a stolen password alone is not enough. Not every second step protects equally. CISA says the only widely available phishing-resistant method is FIDO/WebAuthn, which is what passkeys and security keys use, and that any MFA is better than none. Use a passkey or authenticator where you can, and SMS only when it is all that is offered.

Last updated: 10 Oct 2026.

Sources last checked: 10 Oct 2026.

What 2FA is

CISA defines multifactor authentication as a layered approach to securing your accounts: to get in, you must provide two or more authenticators, such as a password plus something on your phone. Google's version is called 2-Step Verification: something you know (your password) and something you have (your phone, a security key or a backup code).

The common methods

  • Passkey. You sign in with your fingerprint, face scan or phone screen lock instead of typing a password. Google says a passkey cannot be shared, copied, written down or accidentally given to someone else, and recommends passkeys as the default.
  • Security key. A physical device you connect or tap when you sign in.
  • Google prompt. A message on your phone that you approve with a tap. Google recommends it because it is easier than typing a code.
  • Authenticator app. An app that creates short-lived one-time codes. Google notes this works without internet or mobile service.
  • SMS or call code. A 6-digit code sent to your number. It depends on your phone number staying in your hands: see SIM swap scams.
  • Backup codes. One-time codes you save for emergencies.

On ranking: CISA says not all MFA methods give the same protection, and that FIDO/WebAuthn is the only widely available phishing-resistant one. That is why passkeys and security keys sit at the top. Codes you type, whether from an app or an SMS, can still be handed to a fake page by someone who tricks you.

How to turn it on for your Google account

  1. Open your Google Account and go to Security and sign-in.
  2. Under "How you sign in to Google", choose Turn on 2-Step Verification.
  3. Follow the steps, and add a second method such as a passkey or an authenticator app.
  4. Save your backup codes somewhere safe.

For the authenticator app, go to your 2-Step Verification settings and tap Set up authenticator. Google says it may take up to 7 days for Google Authenticator to appear as a sign-in option. If you sign in to your Google Account inside Google Authenticator, your codes sync to your account, so you do not lose them with the phone.

If you lose the phone or the app

Google's page says that if your codes are synced to your Google Account you can remove them by removing the device from your account. If they are not synced, you need to visit each site where you set up the authenticator to remove the old codes and link your new device. That is why backup codes and synced codes matter. See our authenticator recovery guide.

What to do next

  1. Turn on 2-Step Verification for your email first, then your bank and payment apps.
  2. Add a passkey or authenticator app, and keep SMS as a last resort.
  3. Save backup codes. Check our Google account checklist for the rest.
